prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of poetry and prose in Romanian that turns memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: Cărtărescu's case rests on the whole oeuvre rather than a single title. Public knowledge supports an unmistakable voice: dense, recursive, image-driven prose in which body, memory, dream and cosmology form one imaginative system. The Blinding (Orbitor) trilogy and Solenoid carry that project at large scale, and his lyric beginnings in poetry give the prose its musical and metaphoric base. The project appears to widen across decades rather than repeat, which answers the criteria of sustained quality and imaginative depth. The attribution is clean: one writer, one language, and a citation that need not depend on national or political symbolism. After reading my colleagues' openings I keep him first. All six of us placed him first, but I do not treat that convergence as literary evidence. The reasons given by Carlberg, Mattson, Olsson, Palm and Sem-Sandberg (voice, formal ambition, scale of the imaginative project) are the ones I find persuasive on the merits.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the achievement is partly invisible to readers in translation. The Romanian wordplay, rhythm and syntactic patterning that give the prose its force may be flattened, and my view of the poetry and early work is thinner than my view of the major novels. The very long, recursive books also raise a fair question about whether recurrent motifs signal depth or insularity, and whether some of the large works are uneven in pacing. If the committee judged that translation obscures too much of the evidence, a narrower, more compact oeuvre could look easier to assess.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Pierre Michon second, citing compressed, rhythmically exact French prose of exceptional linguistic and formal achievement, and defends intensity over breadth as a strength of quality.
responses.response: I accept that Michon's prose is among the most concentrated on the list, and I ranked him lowest only because of corpus size and translation loss, not because of doubt about the voice. I do not think the small volume disqualifies him. But the case for sustained achievement across a body of work is thinner for him than for Cărtărescu, whose project visibly enlarges across decades and genres. I also cannot judge Michon's syntax in translation, which is the main basis of Mattson's case. I would want a committee reader of the French to say whether the stylistic claim holds up before moving him above my first choice.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Anne Carson second for remaking the boundaries between scholarship, lyric, narrative and visual form, while noting that a citation would need careful framing within Nobel's will and that some effects depend on the book as an object.
responses.response: I share both the admiration and the caveat. Autobiography of Red and Nox show real formal invention joined to emotional force, and I keep Carson as an alternative for that reason. I agree the citation problem is real: if the committee weighs her scholarship and translations alongside the creative work, the scope of the oeuvre becomes harder to define, and I cannot assess the typographic and material effects in the abstract. I would press the question of whether her genre-crossing is the achievement or a vehicle for it. That question is more settled for Cărtărescu, whose innovation lies in the prose itself.

responses.point: Palm ranks Can Xue third, calling her a radically original Chinese-language voice with philosophical seriousness and unusual consistency of method, while flagging limited translation and uncertain variation across her books.
responses.response: Palm's translation concern is mine as well. I ranked Can Xue second because the dream-logic method has few parallels and its strangeness is an internal rigor rather than ornament. But I cannot say how much of the large output is translated, or whether the method deepens or repeats. Sem-Sandberg and Olsson placed her last on the repetition worry, and I take that seriously rather than dismiss it. I keep her as an alternative, but I would want better evidence of development across the corpus before putting her ahead of a writer whose variety is clearer to me.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Raúl Zurita second, for large poetic sequences and landscape-scale interventions that turn historical suffering into collective memorial form, while asking how far non-textual interventions count as literary achievement.
responses.response: I did not rank Zurita in my opening, and I agree that his poetic ambition and scale are real. Olsson's own question is the sticking point for me: the case must be made from the poems' language, and poetry in translation is the weakest ground for such a judgment. The historical weight of the subject should not stand in for formal evaluation. I would be open to hearing a reading of the Spanish that shows what the translations miss, but on the evidence I have, I cannot place him above Cărtărescu.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose texture, wordplay and rhythm reaches readers in translation, and whether the translated corpus fairly represents the poetry and early work.
Whether the repetition of motifs and the length of the major novels are best read as sustained depth or as limits on range.
Corpus coverage is uneven: the major novels are better known to me than the poetry and shorter prose, and I have not independently verified any text.
Whether the dream-logic method of Can Xue develops across a large partly untranslated oeuvre, and how the committee would weigh Carson's hybrid, scholarly and translated work in framing a citation.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I have no documented personal or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. My ties to committee colleagues are collegial service only and do not require recusal.
